unit.title: Reading a trail description
unit.summary: Miles, gain, grade, pace and the vocabulary of difficulty.

lessons.title: Miles are not the whole story
lessons.objective: You can explain why elevation gain matters as much as distance.

payload.prompt: A 6-mile hike with 2,000 ft gain feels roughly like?

explanation.correct: The gain adds time and effort. Naismith's rule suggests 2,000 ft gains over an hour, turning 6 miles into 10-mile equivalent difficulty.
explanation.incorrect: Elevation gain multiplies effort. The 2,000 feet of climbing dominates the hike, making it feel much longer than the mileage alone suggests.

payload.prompt: Two hikes: 10 miles flat or 5 miles with 3,000 ft gain. Which is typically longer?

options.text: The 10-mile flat hike
The 5-mile hike with 3,000 ft gain
They take about the same time
Impossible to compare without knowing terrain

explanation.correct: The steep one. 3,000 feet of gain adds about 1.5 hours of hiking time by Naismith's rule, making the shorter, steeper hike longer than the flat one.
explanation.incorrect: Gain is the hidden variable. Distance alone doesn't tell the story. The 5-mile steep hike takes longer than the 10-mile flat one.
explanation.sayThisLine: Only five miles? What's the elevation gain? That changes everything.

payload.prompt: A trail climbs 500 ft in half a mile. Is this steep?

options.text: Not steep at all, just a casual climb
Moderately steep, a sustained grade
Very steep, about 18% grade
Needs more information to judge

explanation.correct: That's a 18% grade: 500 ft rise over 2,640 ft horizontal distance (half a mile). Eighteen percent is noticeably steep, and your quads will feel it.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is rise over run. Five hundred feet in half a mile is steep—expect a grinding climb and tired legs.
explanation.sayThisLine: The trail climbs five hundred feet in half a mile. This is going to be steep.

payload.prompt: A trail listing says 8 miles with 800 ft gain. How many hours?

explanation.correct: By Naismith's rule: 8 miles at 3 mph = 2 hours, plus 800 ft ÷ 2,000 ft per hour = 0.4 hours = about 3 hours moving time. Add breaks and you're looking 3.5 to 4.
explanation.incorrect: Use Naismith's rule: one hour per three miles, plus one hour per 2,000 feet. Eight miles takes about 2.5 hours of pure movement, plus the gain.

payload.prompt: Why does a trail description list elevation gain separately from mileage?

options.text: It's redundant; gain is built into mileage
Gain matters more than distance for time and effort
It's only important for steep trails
Trail builders have to track both for regulatory reasons

explanation.correct: Gain tells you how much climbing to expect. Two hikes with the same mileage can feel completely different based on elevation gain.
explanation.incorrect: Distance and gain are independent. Six miles with 3,000 feet is a slog; six miles with 200 feet is a cruise. Both are six miles but totally different hikes.
explanation.sayThisLine: The gain is the number that actually tells you how hard it is.

lessons.title: How steep is steep
lessons.objective: You can turn rise and run into a grade and feel what it means.

payload.prompt: A hillside climbs 100 ft in 400 ft horizontal distance. What percent grade?

explanation.correct: Grade = (rise ÷ run) × 100. Here: (100 ÷ 400) × 100 = 25%. That's steep; your breathing gets hard.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is the ratio of vertical rise to horizontal distance. 100 feet up over 400 feet horizontal = 25 percent grade.

payload.prompt: Which section is steeper?

diagram.alt: Two slopes: left gradual, right steep.

explanation.correct: The right covers more vertical in the same space. That's steeper.
explanation.incorrect: Grade is the climb angle. The right rises sharply—higher grade, harder.

payload.prompt: A 10% grade trail: roughly how much elevation in one mile?

explanation.correct: One mile = 5,280 feet. Ten percent grade means 0.10 × 5,280 = 528 feet of elevation. That's noticeable but not extreme.
explanation.incorrect: Grade × horizontal distance = elevation. A 10% grade over a mile (5,280 horizontal feet) equals about 528 vertical feet.

payload.prompt: Which grade feels easier to hike?

options.text: 3% grade
8% grade
15% grade
25% grade

explanation.correct: A 3% grade is gentle. Eight percent gets tiring, 15% is steep, 25% is brutal. Lower grade = easier hiking and less knee stress.
explanation.incorrect: Lower percentage means a gentler slope. Three percent is barely noticeable; twenty-five percent will make your legs burn.

payload.prompt: You read a trail climbs 1,500 ft in 2 miles. Approximately what's the average grade?

options.text: 5% grade
14% grade
28% grade
50% grade

explanation.correct: Two miles = 10,560 horizontal feet. (1,500 ÷ 10,560) × 100 = 14% average. That's sustained climbing, expect to work.
explanation.incorrect: Do the math: 1,500 ft rise over two miles (10,560 ft horizontal) is a 14% average grade. That's moderately steep.

lessons.title: Planning with Naismith
lessons.objective: You can estimate hiking time from distance and gain.

payload.prompt: A trail is 9 miles with 1,200 ft gain. How long by Naismith?

explanation.correct: Naismith: 9 miles at 3 mph = 3 hours. Plus 1,200 ft ÷ 2,000 ft per hour = 0.6 hours. Total ≈ 3.6 hours. Round to 4-4.5 for real-world pace.
explanation.incorrect: Use the rule: 1 hour per 3 miles, plus 1 hour per 2,000 feet of gain. Nine miles = 3 hours, 1,200 feet = 0.6 hours, total about 3.5 to 4 hours.

payload.prompt: Complete Naismith's rule.
payload.template: {{one}} hour per {{three}} miles, plus {{one2}} hour per 2,000 feet of gain.

explanation.correct: That is Naismith's rule: distance and gain set your baseline time.
explanation.incorrect: One hour per three miles plus one hour per 2,000 feet of climbing.

payload.prompt: 4 hours moving time by Naismith. Add time for breaks, lunch and photos. Total?

explanation.correct: Real-world hiking adds contingency. Add 30% to 50% to Naismith time for breaks, lunch, photos and slower real pace. Four hours becomes 5 to 6 hours.
explanation.incorrect: Moving time is just walking. Total time includes stops for food, water, views and photos. Most hikers add 30 to 50 percent.

payload.prompt: Naismith assumes a hiking speed of roughly how many miles per hour on flat terrain?

options.text: 1 mile per hour
2 miles per hour
3 miles per hour
5 miles per hour

explanation.correct: Naismith's baseline is 3 mph on flat ground, a sustainable pace for most hikers. Steeper terrain or tired legs slow you down.
explanation.incorrect: The rule uses 3 mph as the baseline on flat terrain. That is neither power-hiking nor strolling—a real-world pace most people can sustain.

payload.prompt: Your plan says 3.5 hours moving time. You leave at 7 AM. When do you plan to return?

options.text: 10:30 AM, right at 3.5 hours
11:00 AM, with minimal stops
12:00 PM to 1:00 PM, realistic pace with breaks
Impossible to say without knowing the terrain

explanation.correct: Add 30 to 50% to moving time for the real world: lunch, water stops, photos and pace variations. Three and a half hours moving = 5 to 5.5 hours total. Back by noon or one.
explanation.incorrect: Moving time is not total time. Plan for extra: you will stop for food, water and the view. Double the moving time or add 50 percent to be realistic.

lessons.title: Real pace, fantasy pace
lessons.objective: You can adjust pace for terrain, pack and group.

payload.prompt: On steep, rocky terrain, average pace drops to roughly what?

explanation.correct: Steep, rough terrain cuts pace in half or more: 1 to 1.5 mph is realistic. Your feet work harder, rocks slow you, and you rest more often.
explanation.incorrect: Terrain matters hugely. Rocky slopes, scree and steep grades drop pace from 3 mph (flat) to 1 to 1.5 mph or slower.

payload.prompt: Which factors slowest on a hike?

options.text: Heat and humidity
A heavy pack
Rock scrambles or scree
All of the above, roughly equally

explanation.correct: Rock scrambles and scree stop you cold. You move one step at a time, carefully. Gain slows pace, but rough terrain slows it more.
explanation.incorrect: Difficult terrain—scree, boulders, rock scrambles—is the biggest pace killer. Even fitter hikers slow to one step at a time.
explanation.sayThisLine: We did a section of scree and dropped to a mile per hour or less.

payload.prompt: You are at 8,000 ft elevation. Your pace drops to roughly what percent of sea-level pace?

explanation.correct: At altitude, breathing is harder and your body works less efficiently. Expect 70 to 80% of your sea-level pace, and slower as you go higher.
explanation.incorrect: Altitude slows everyone. At 8,000 feet, most hikers move at 70 to 80% of their normal pace. Higher altitude slows you further.

payload.prompt: The group rule for pace is?

options.text: The fastest person sets the pace
Everyone keeps up or stays home
The slowest person sets the pace and no one gets left behind
Split up into faster and slower groups

explanation.correct: Group hiking means the pace of the slowest. Nobody gets left behind, and nobody waits alone out of earshot. That is how groups stay safe and together.
explanation.incorrect: The group moves at the pace of the slowest person. This keeps everyone together, builds group cohesion and keeps someone from getting lost or injured alone.

payload.prompt: A 20-pound pack slows your pace by roughly what percent compared to no pack?

explanation.correct: Twenty pounds slows most hikers by 10 to 20 percent. Lighter packs are faster; heavier packs slow you more and tire legs faster.
explanation.incorrect: Pack weight adds up. Twenty pounds might slow you 15 percent or so on typical terrain. Steep or rocky terrain magnifies the impact.

lessons.title: What moderate actually means
lessons.objective: You can explain why difficulty labels vary and what the class scale describes.

payload.prompt: Match the Yosemite class to the hiking challenge.

pairs.definition: Walking on a trail; no special skills needed
Hiking off-trail, simple rock scramble, hands in pockets
Hands-on scrambling, exposed drops, must watch placement

distractorDefinitions: Running at high speed on a rocky summit

explanation.summary: The class scale goes from hike to scramble to climb. Class 3 is where hands matter. Class 4 is where ropes come out.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: The trail is moderate on AllTrails but strenuous on the park site.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: Difficulty ratings differ by app and agency
Check miles and elevation gain, not labels
Moderate and strenuous mean the same thing

payload.translation: Difficulty ratings vary widely across apps. One's moderate is another's strenuous. Check objective metrics instead.

followUps.line: Look at miles and feet of gain, not the label alone.
followUps.why: The numbers tell you more than the subjective rating.

followUps.line: Ask locals or read trip reports for real feedback.
followUps.why: Recent experience beats any rating system.

followUps.line: Ask what moderate means to her before comparing.
followUps.why: Everyone's scale is different; clarify first.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Ratings are subjective. Asking 'What does moderate mean?' shows honesty, not ignorance.

payload.prompt: A trail labeled class 2 scramble means?

options.text: Hiking on a trail; safe for kids and dogs
Off-trail hiking with simple rock scrambling; hands rarely needed
Hands-on scrambling with exposure; serious and high-risk
Roped climbing, requires technical skills

explanation.correct: Class 2 is off-trail scrambling; you might use your hands to balance but do not really need them. Exposure is minimal to moderate.
explanation.incorrect: Class 2 is the first level of scramble: some rock work, mostly staying upright, hands used occasionally. Not dangerous, but not a pure hiking trail.

payload.prompt: Which is most useful for comparing hikes objectively?

options.text: An app's difficulty rating (easy/moderate/hard)
Total distance in miles
Elevation gain in feet and the class scale
Recent trip reports from other hikers

explanation.correct: Elevation gain and the class scale tell you the real story: how far you climb and what terrain you face. Apps rate differently; numbers never lie.
explanation.incorrect: Distance alone misleads. Six miles with 100 feet feels easy; six miles with 3,000 feet feels hard. Gain + class scale is objective.

payload.prompt: On a class 3 scramble, what is most important?

options.text: Speed; get through it quickly
Testing hand and foot placement; fall risk is real
Bringing trekking poles for balance
Wearing a helmet for safety

explanation.correct: Class 3 has exposure and fall risk. You must think through placement, move carefully and test holds before committing. Rushing kills.
explanation.incorrect: Class 3 demands attention and care. A fall can hurt badly. Test every hold, move deliberately and respect the exposure.

lessons.title: Trail, route, exposure, water
lessons.objective: You can read a description for red flags: routes, exposure, unreliable water.

payload.prompt: Trail description: 'Follow cairns across open rock for two miles.' Is this a trail or a route?

scene.alt: Bare rock with small stone cairns marking a path. No tread visible.

explanation.correct: No maintained tread, just cairns. That is a route. You navigate by rock, landmarks and markers, not a worn path.
explanation.incorrect: A trail has maintained tread; a route is a line across terrain marked by cairns or landmarks. This is a route, and navigation is part of the game.

payload.prompt: A guide says 'Route, needs navigation.' Go solo if new to navigation?

options.text: Sure, routes are easy
Yes, with offline maps and a GPS track
Go with someone experienced
Avoid it; get formal training first

explanation.correct: Routes demand navigation. Go with someone experienced. A trail has tread; a route has only your judgment.
explanation.incorrect: Routes need map and compass work, terrain reading and decision-making. Learn with a mentor first.

payload.prompt: What does 'exposure' mean in trail descriptions?

options.text: How long the hike takes in direct sun
Steep drop-offs beside the route where a fall is serious
How wet and muddy the trail gets
How much rain or wind is forecast

explanation.correct: Exposure = steep drop-offs beside your path. A fall is bad. Exposure does not mean danger on a wide trail; it means commitment and consequences.
explanation.incorrect: Exposure is the vertical hazard: cliffs or steep drops beside the route. High exposure means a slip could be serious. It demands attention and care.

payload.prompt: Trail says: 'Water at mile 3 (seasonal). Do not rely on it.' Can you plan a 12-mile day using only that source?

scene.alt: A trail map with a water source marked at mile 3 labeled 'seasonal'.

explanation.correct: Seasonal means it may be dry when you go. The guide says do not rely on it. Bring all water or verify the source first via recent trip reports.
explanation.incorrect: When a guide says not to rely on water, believe it. Seasonal sources can be empty. Plan and carry what you need.

payload.prompt: Creek at 4 mi (reliable), spring at 8 mi (seasonal), dry for last 4. Carry?

options.text: One liter, there's water at mile 4
Enough from mile 4 to the end, plus a backup filter
Just download the route, water is always there
Two liters total, water is listed so it's reliable

explanation.correct: Reliable creek at 4: fill there. Seasonal spring at 8: skip it. Dry for 4: carry from 4 to end.
explanation.incorrect: Trust 'reliable' and fill there. Skip 'seasonal.' Carry what you need for the dry section.
